native_result.query: Does increased time preference leads to higher BMI?
native_result.HypoA: Higher time preference associated with higher BMI for 1989 data.
native_result.WorkflowA:
1. Selected appropriate variables from the raw data
e.g.: Height: Height of respondent on 1985 instead of 1981.
      Income: Total net family income, 1989 (There are many other income variables in the raw data)
      Age:    Age of respondent at 1989 (Derived from Age at 1979).
Data Transformation:
2. Replaced -1 to -5 values (unavailable data) with NaN
3. Imputed the missing values in the AGE and INCOME variable with mean.
4. AGE_1989 had missing values, hence derived the variable as [AGE_1979 + 10]
5. Created a BMI variable using: bmi = (weight) * 0.453592 / (height) * 0.0254
6. Divided the Family income variable by 1000$ (Mentioned in the paper)
7. Created an AGE^2 variable (From the paper)
8. One-hot encoded RACE variable into BLACK and HISPANIC
9. One-hot encooded GENDER variable into MALE and FEMALE
10. Selected 'Was more money put into or taken out of R/spouse savings since last interview, 1989' as the Time Preference variable.
  DISSAVED = 1 if 'TOOK MORE MONEY OUT' else 0
  SAMESAVE = 1 if 'NO SAVINGS' or 'NO CHANGE' else 0
11. Dropped the unimportant columns for replication
12. DISSAVED and SAMESAVE as independent variables and BMI as dependent variable
13. Fit an OLS Regression Model
native_result.HypoB: Increased time preference (proxied by more dissaving-oriented savings behavior in the 1989 NLSY79 interview, 1-4 index, higher = more time preference) is associated with higher BMI in 1992: +0.298 BMI units per index step (95% CI 0.169-0.426, std beta 0.06, p<0.001, n=6473), monotone category means 25.56 -> 27.13, robust to dropping the 'no savings' category, alternative height calibration, class-rank control, and a reverse-temporal 1981-BMI check; association only, not causal.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Read data/nls_raw.csv (12,686 x 61). 2) Unit calibration: weights confirmed as pounds (BMI plausibility 26.3 vs 57.7); 1981 height scale calibrated to meters via 1985 inch-height (raw/3.048/100; validated by OLS-calibration alternative). 3) Constructed BMI1992 (primary) and BMI1981 (robustness); TP index = 1989 savings-direction item (higher = more time preference); net saving flow (winsorized) as robustness TP. 4) Covariates: age1989, sex, race dummies, grade1979 (sentinels dropped), ever-incarceration (JAIL=5 any year or pre-1980 sentence), ASVAB composite (standardized), log family income 1989. 5) OLS with HC1 robust SEs, listwise deletion (n=6473), standardized beta via z-scored re-fit; cross-validated with statsmodels. 6) Complete-vs-incomplete attrition comparison; sensitivity dropping 'no savings' category.

sub_hypo.text: Higher time preference, proxied by a more dissaving-oriented 1989 savings-behavior index, is associated with higher BMI in 1992 among NLSY79 participants. The association is not causal.
sub_hypo.context: NLSY79 participants with complete data after listwise deletion (n=6473); 1989 savings behavior predicts 1992 BMI in OLS models with HC1 robust standard errors.

sub_hypo.relations: Positive association: each step on the 1–4 time-preference index (higher = greater time preference) corresponds to +0.298 BMI units in 1992 (95% CI 0.169–0.426; standardized beta 0.06; p<0.001). Category mean BMI increases monotonically from 25.56 to 27.13. Models adjust for age, sex, race, education, ever-incarceration, standardized ASVAB composite, and log family income. BMI uses weights calibrated as pounds and 1981 height converted to meters using 1985 inch-height calibration. The association is robust to excluding 'no savings,' alternative height calibration, class-rank control, and a reverse-temporal 1981-BMI check; winsorized net saving flow is an alternative time-preference measure in the workflow. No causal interpretation is asserted.
